articles.title: Malaysia to send thousands of migrants back to Myanmar as PM acknowledges junta’s ‘atrocities’
articles.summary: Prime minister Anwar Ibrahim’s announcement comes days after the ICJ found Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya minority
body: Malaysia says it will send thousands of migrants and refugees back to Myanmar, despite acknowledging that many asylum seekers in the country had been victims of “atrocities” carried ​out by the junta in Naypyidaw.
The announcement comes just days after the UN’s highest court ruled Myanmar had committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

Malaysia’s prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim, said on Tuesday that the deportations were in line with advice from the international court of justice (ICJ), which was “to guarantee a safe and dignified return” for those fleeing persecution, and his country had not abandoned its principles of upholding the rights of the people of Myanmar.
Related: Malaysia begins Myanmar repatriations despite warnings from UN and rights groups
The UN has previously warned that migrants sent back to Myanmar could face a dangerous homecoming.

It is unclear how many Rohingya, a Muslim minority group, are among those facing deportation. However, the Rohingya make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the UN. Many of the Rohingya escaped to Malaysia during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.

Anwar acknowledged that many asylum seekers in Malaysia were “victims of atrocities carried ​out by the Myanmar regime”, but said Malaysia could ‌no longer afford to host refugees. Hoping for them to be resettled in third countries had not worked, he said.

Many in Malaysia have grown increasingly frustrated by ‌the presence of refugees in the country, saying that hosting them has become a financial burden and a security risk, with a rise in anti-migrant sentiment in the country.

On Tuesday Anwar told Malaysia’s parliament that three naval ships would return 1,500 people in December, with an additional 5,303 people flown back by aircraft at the expense of the Myanmar government.
Tuesday’s announcement follows last week’s ICJ ruling in The Hague that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ had never previously found a state responsible for genocide, and the judgment ended a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang rapes and burnt-down villages.
In its judgment, the ICJ said Myanmar authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.
Related: When you see smoke, run: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
In September, Malaysia began sending back a group of about 1,500 Myanmar nationals as it launched its contested repatriation plan.
Malaysia’s government said in a statement at the time that the repatriation was necessary to resolve the “legacy issue” of foreign asylum seekers in Malaysia – of which it said 95% were from Myanmar.

“This long-standing issue has imposed a significant financial burden on the nation, triggered serious social crises, and created tangible security threats for the Malaysian people,” the statement said.
The UN had urged Malaysia to stop that repatriation, saying nobody should be deported to Myanmar, given the severity of the situation on the ground.
In late October, the Malaysian government said it would seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned were being held in military detention.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Ebikes, screens and failing manners pose challenge for Dutch cycling culture
articles.summary: Awareness campaign reminds public ‘traffic is a team sport’ amid less civility and more collisions on roads
body: For decades the Netherlands has been famed for its proud cycling culture, with a network of 23,000 miles of bike paths used by everyone from children under eight to adults over 80.

In recent years, however, like so many countries around the world, it has seen a dramatic change in the type of vehicles using those lanes: no longer the preserve of pedal bikes, they are used by all manner of two-wheeled vehicles including electric cargo bikes, thick-tyred “fatbikes”, speed pedelecs, electric scooters and even some micro cars.

Throw smartphones into the mix as well, say critics, and the result is clear: less space, more conflict, less civility and more collisions. According to the Netherlands Institute for Transport Policy Analysis, the annual number of cyclist deaths increased by more than 50% between 2015 and 2025.
What is needed, say some, are new rules of the road (or, at least, path). Last week, the Dutch government sent a bill to parliament proposing mandatory helmets for under-18s on ebikes.

The moves are welcomed by those who feel that things need to change. As one resident, Patrick van den Hoven, wrote in the Amsterdam newspaper Het Parool this month: “Let’s call a spade a spade: [ebikes] are vehicles with a motor, which, as far as I am concerned, we should treat as motor vehicles.”
The city’s bike lanes now resembled “a permanent traffic experiment”, he said, adding: “The bicycle made our country great. It would be a shame if it eventually fell victim to electric progress.”

Another city, Leiden, launched a public awareness campaign earlier this month to remind everyone that “traffic is a team sport”. It has the Netherlands’ highest number of bike accidents per head, and cyclist injuries have risen by more than half since 2018.

“This campaign aims to say: guys, watch out for one another,” said Julius Terpstra, the deputy mayor for spatial planning and mobility. “We see more people on bikes, more older people on bikes due to the ageing population, and more different vehicles, when once the Netherlands only had the Gazelle [a famed brand of pedal bike]. We see national trends here too: the rise of the electric bike, more telephone use, and also drug use.”

According to Florrie de Pater, a board member of the Fietsersbond Amsterdam cycling union, there has been a notable decline in road manners. “There is less consideration for one another and less empathy among cyclists, perhaps also because we live in an individualistic world where everything has to go fast, fast, fast,” she said.

Romee Nicolai, the bicycle mayor of Amsterdam, believes some people have forgotten that the extensive network of dedicated cycle paths was created after a wave of activism sparked by road deaths in the 1970s.

“People have been cycling for hundreds of years, but we need to acknowledge that this cannot continue if we don’t give it attention,” she said. “You can’t grow plants if you don’t give them attention and water, and it’s the same with cycling. That means public debate, and financial means from government to create a safe cycling environment too.”

Some older people have told her they are too afraid of an accident to get on their bicycles, while one in five children are growing up without a cycling culture. “We need to acknowledge that we are actually losing those cyclists,” Nicolai said.

The National Institute for Public Health and the Environment found in a recent study that fewer Dutch young adults were doing the recommended daily amount of movement, partly owing to less general cycling and the rise of the electric bike.

Jasper Reenalda, a human movement scientist at the University of Twente, has some concerns about the impact of more ebike use, particularly if children lose a low-impact exercise that was once built into everyday life.

“Our whole infrastructure was built around bikes, so children bike to school, they bike to sports, they bike to all kinds of social activities,” he said. “It was always very easy for Dutch children to reach the norms of active, minimally active behaviour. If children are switching to ebikes, and that’s the trend, it is more challenging to reach the minimum number of active minutes to stay healthy.”

However, some experts warn it is easy to stereotype certain groups – such as “fatbike” users – for causing the tensions. Clara Glachant, a researcher in micromobility at Eindhoven University of Technology, said electric bikes could have a positive role in “expanding cycling to groups that do not cycle”.

Meredith Glaser, the chief executive of the Urban Cycling Institute in Amsterdam, said four in 10 cyclists who died in recent years were in a collision with a car. “Any pointing of fingers towards cyclists is an excellent scapegoat for the uncomfortable reality that cars and trucks are still taking up the majority of public space and causing the most harm to the environment and to human bodies,” she said.

articles.title: ‘Produce a good result by any means’: how AI is testing South Korea’s exam obsession
articles.summary: South Korea has made exams a career-defining way to level the playing field, but AI has plunged the system into chaos
body: “I have never worn glasses in my life,” Yun Jeong-hu says to the camera, holding up a tax law textbook, and flipping through pages plastered with notes and dotted with highlighted sections.

In the 22-minute video, the 25-year-old talks viewers through his study methods, naming his tutors, describing watching recorded lectures until 3am, and solving a corporate tax question live and unrehearsed.
Related: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
The first pair of glasses he ever put on, he says, was for a job interview, because he worried he looked too young.

Yun had posted the footage because he came second in South Korea’s national tax accountant exam, amid widespread claims circulating online that the exam’s high scorers had cheated by using AI smartglasses.

In other recent exams, successful candidates posted images of used-up pen refills and annotated textbooks to prove they had studied. One noted they had had laser eye surgery two years earlier, preempting any suggestion they would use smartglasses.

“It’s truly deplorable to see the hard work of everyone preparing for or passing exams of any kind being disparaged,” Yun wrote under his video, asking people to stop spreading groundless speculation.
Claims of cheating are a regular fact of life in South Korea, which places career-defining emphasis on exams, but this year they have been turbocharged by the opportunities that AI affords.

Last week, officials sent alerts normally reserved for air raids and nuclear attacks to every phone in the country in a bid to root out cheats smuggling in a device to the suneung, the gruelling eight-hour university entrance exam. The education ministry said 111 candidates were caught with electronic devices, of whom 54 were exposed by the alerts themselves.

The country’s leaders have been grappling with the new tech challenge: president Lee Jae Myung promised a reward of at least 100m won ($74,000) for successful tipoffs about cheating. On Sunday, South Korea’s education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, resigned amid the disruption caused by last-minute changes brought in to tackle AI-assisted cheating in the suneung.

“Because a single test determines a lifetime’s economic position and social recognition, there is extreme pressure to produce a good result by any means,” says Sangchin Chun, a professor of sociology at Sogang University, adding exams have become mythologised as “the only remaining bastion of fairness”.

That extreme pressure took a dark turn this month. One man who scored full marks in a recent national law school admission exam was accused of using AI. He had said he would answer his critics by publicly answering part of this year’s suneung in real time but he never appeared at the event last week. He was later found dead in a Seoul motel. The allegations against him had not been established.

The roots of South Korea’s exam obsession lie partly in the economic insecurity that followed the 1997 Asian financial crisis, says Kim Dong-chun, a sociologist and author of a study of South Korea’s exam meritocracy.

Family wealth and connections had long shaped who gets ahead in South Korea, but as job security became harder to find, exams became the accepted way of allocating shrinking opportunities, he argues, because no other procedure felt fair.
In 2019, the then justice minister, Cho Kuk, became embroiled in a scandal – and was later jailed – for forging academic credentials to get his children into prestigious schools and universities.

Once again, exams were seen as a way to level the playing field, and the Cho scandal prompted the government to press major universities in Seoul to allocate at least 40% of their places on the basis of entrance exam scores.

Choi Hang-seop, a professor of sociology at Kookmin University, told Yonhap news agency that South Korea had truly become a survival-of-the-fittest society, one that is harsh on those who fall slightly short and one in which people come to believe that doing well in the suneung or a state exam is the only way to survive.

Amid fears that essay coaching could favour wealthier families, the suneung university exam is almost entirely multiple choice and marked by machine, with no essay, interview or coursework. It is treated as the ultimate equaliser: the one place where everybody sits the same paper at the same time, anonymously.

However, reformers have long argued that the exam’s format is the problem. In August, the national education commission’s chair, Cha Jeong-in, said multiple choice had reached its limits and essay assessment was unavoidable, but the commission could not agree and the plan was pushed back. A redesign of the suneung is already under way for 2028, but the multi-choice format itself will be unchanged.
Chun says a system of assessment built around memorisation and problem-solving had been overtaken by the AI technology now in candidates’ hands and that the cheating had flourished in the gap.
The debate over how to respond, he says, remains focused either on stricter invigilation and punishment or on modernising the system through computer-based testing.
Belief in the myth of meritocracy remains firm, he says, along with the pride in the idea that “the examination republic is still the best there is”.

Park Do-soon, who led the design of the suneung and became the first head of the body that runs it, is no longer convinced. “I don’t see any reason for humans to sit the kind of exam where AI can get the answer in one go”, he told Hankook Ilbo.

articles.title: South Korea tells island residents to take shelter after Russian military aircraft approach
articles.summary: The order was issued after aircraft entered the country’s air defence identification zone over the island of Ulleungdo
body: Residents of a remote South Korean island were ordered to take shelter on Tuesday morning after several Russian military aircraft came close to entering its airspace, prompting a pre-emptive alert from the military that anticipated a violation.
The defence ministry said it would summon the Russian defence attaché on Tuesday afternoon to lodge a strong protest.

The joint chiefs of staff (JCS) said the aircraft had entered the country’s air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan – known in South Korea as the East Sea – and approached the island of Ulleungdo. It did not specify how many Russian aircraft were involved, but South Korean air force jets were scrambled before the aircraft left.

A JCS spokesperson, Jang Do-young, said the aircraft had approached “to the point just before violating Ulleungdo’s airspace” and that, because military aircraft move very fast, a violation was anticipated.
Related: The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and Russia
The alert was issued pre-emptively to protect residents, he said.

The interior ministry issued the emergency alert at 7.52am to residents of Ulleungdo, a volcanic island of about 8,700 people 120km off the east coast, telling them to take shelter. The English portion of the message read: “EVACUATION, AIR RAID”.

Television broadcasts were interrupted by on-screen warnings telling residents to “prepare to evacuate to a nearby underground shelter facility and listen to broadcasting”. The alert was lifted at 7.55am.

On the island, sirens sounded and residents reportedly heard the noise of fighter jets. Jeong Hae-seung, 41, who was working on a building site, told the Hankyoreh newspaper he ran out of his workplace the moment the text arrived.
“I went outside wondering what on earth was going on, and the civil defence broadcast was playing, but I couldn’t make out what it was saying,” he said.
Baek Un-bae, who lives on the island, told broadcaster YTN that an elderly resident had telephoned him asking whether war had broken out.
“Older people have no access to the media, so all they hear is the warning broadcast and they are too alarmed to know what to do,” he said.
Others said they did not hear the sirens at all, with windows shut against the cold and strong winds blowing.
A second message, sent by North Gyeongsang province, which administers Ulleungdo, said a flying object “presumed to be a North Korean aircraft” had left the danger zone.
The province said it had mistakenly taken the wording from its routine drill messages, changed only the time and sent it in error.
Jang described the alert as unusual but said he could not confirm whether it was the first of its kind.
Tuesday’s incident was the fourth known entry by Russian military aircraft into the zone this year and the second in a week.

An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace, but countries establish such zones beyond their own airspace to identify incoming military flights early. While submitting a flight plan in advance is international practice, entering an identification zone without prior notification does not in itself violate international law.
Russia argues that the Korean zone has no basis in international law and does not recognise Seoul’s authority over it, and has repeatedly flown into it without notice.
According to data submitted to parliament, about 60 Russian entries without prior notification were recorded in the five years to 2024, compared with about 430 by Chinese aircraft.

Seoul previously summoned Russia’s defence attaché in March 2025 after eight entries in 10 days. At the time, it was the first such summons since a Russian aircraft violated South Korean airspace in 2019 and South Korean jets fired warning shots.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv’s strike on Russian ships in Benghazi condemned by Libya’s UN-backed government
articles.summary: Tripoli-based foreign ministry demands explanation from Kyiv; Guardian analysis identifies more than 460,000 Russian deaths linked to the war. What we know on day 1,735
body: Libya’s foreign ministry condemned an attack on two Russian ships near the eastern city of Benghazi claimed by Ukraine, demanding an explanation from Kyiv. The attacks caused the Russian corvette Merkury to explode and sink at the port of Benghazi, while a dry cargo vessel was also hit. Ukraine said Russia was using it to transport weapons. The Tripoli-based foreign ministry of Libya’s UN-recognised government condemned the “conduct of any foreign military operations within Libyan territory or territorial waters”.

Ukraine confirmed it deployed naval drones in the strikes on the two Russian vessels off Libya, Peter Beaumont reports. Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”. The Ukrainian president released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

A Guardian analysis of more than 11m Russian death certificates obtained by hacking groups has given the most detailed picture yet of Russia’s losses in Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Guardian identified more than 460,000 deaths linked to the war between the start of the invasion in February 2022 and September 2026. War became the leading cause of death in Russian men under 65 last year. The real toll is likely to be higher. The deaths of missing soldiers are often registered months or years later, when bodies are recovered or courts declare men dead, and the records thin out sharply in 2026, even though the fighting has remained exceptionally deadly.

Figures from the cache of certificates reveal more than 1,000 Russian soldiers recorded as having died by suicide since the start of the full-scale invasion. The deaths of a further 885 soldiers in or near Ukraine were recorded as firearm-related injuries of “undetermined intent”, a classification that experts say can conceal suicides and that was used in several cases independently identified by the Guardian as suicides. The data, which analysts say almost certainly underestimates the true number of suicides, offers a rare and previously unreported glimpse of the strain on Russia’s armed forces nearly five years into a war in which heavy losses and harsh discipline have sapped morale.

A Russian unmanned aerial vehicle briefly violated Polish ⁠airspace during ⁠a ​nighttime attack on western Ukraine, the Polish armed forces ⁠said. An authorisation was given to ⁠shoot down the object but after ​it ‌changed its ‌course to head east, “taking into ‌account the potential threat to civilians and the possible consequences of shooting down the object”, a decision was ‌made to refrain from using weapons, the post on X said. Three ​Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland on Friday, adding to fears ⁠that Russia’s war in Ukraine could ​spill ​over into Nato ​territory.

Britain’s defence secretary has said restrictions on the use of SpaceX’s satellite communications by Ukraine’s military have caused concern among European ⁠governments and damaged trust in the company’s services. “This has been a topic of conversation among defence ministers right across Europe: it has really dented confidence and trust,” ⁠Wes Streeting said during ⁠a visit to ​Kyiv. Ukraine said earlier this month that its military units had recorded significant disruptions to the Starshield military communication system provided by SpaceX, affecting the entire frontline ⁠and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. Streeting said: “We are owed a clear explanation about those service interruptions: why and how they happened and why customers should be confident that they will get the service that they pay for.”

The World Food Programme’s executive director, Luke Lindberg, has warned that shipping chokepoints linked to wars in the Middle East and Ukraine could raise the agency’s costs by $727m by mid-2027, threatening food aid for 7.3 million more people. He said constraints on food ⁠exports were compounded by climate shocks like El Niño. “It’s an unthinkable scenario, and it could not come at a worse time,” said Lindberg, a former US agriculture official, urging diplomats to focus ⁠on trying to find rapid solutions to ensure 10m tons of Ukrainian and Russian grain that were already in silos reached people in need.

articles.title: Natural beauty made this New Zealand tourist village. Now it threatens its existence
articles.summary: Famed for its nearby glacier, Franz Josef village faces ‘catastrophic’ flooding and deaths if action not taken to manage the Waiho River
body: The small village of Franz Josef sits on the rugged west coast of New Zealand’s South Island, its natural beauty providing the drawcard for a million tourists to pack its hotels, spas and restaurants every year.

But that drawcard – which has turned it into a hotspot for everything from hiking to kayaking and made it one of the country’s most popular destinations – may change the course of the village’s fate once again.
Its collection of buildings lies in the shadow of the famed Franz Josef glacier, on an alpine fault and beside the Waiho River, a globally rare braided river. And the river is rising.
Related: ‘Slipping through our fingers’: New Zealand scientists distraught at scale of glacier loss

The latest technical report, released in September, shows the Waiho is rapidly rising and changing course – several years earlier than previously predicted – and scientists warn that Franz Josef is at risk of “catastrophic” flooding and deaths if action is not taken to release its waters. The report shows the original 10-year plan to release water from the river needs to be brought forward.

“If the full force of the Waiho goes through the township, then the structures, buildings – whatever is in its way – will be significantly damaged, if not destroyed,” says Prof Ian Fuller, a fluvial geomorphologist and spokesperson for the independent Waiho technical advisory group, set up to advise the West Coast regional council.
“We’ve now got seven years ... essentially we need to be doing 10 years work in seven,” Fuller said.
Since the report’s release, scientists have been calling for urgent intervention to prevent a disaster, which has prompted local authorities to accelerate their river management plans.
While links to climate change affecting the river are tenuous at this stage, global warming and El Niño will bring more rainfall and the potential of floods, Fuller says.

Adding to the risk, there is a 75% probability of a magnitude eight earthquake within the next 50 years, according to Earth Sciences NZ. A rupture could trigger flooding, landslides and cause “wholesale destruction of the town,” Fuller says, describing the damage as “potentially catastrophic”.

But he was quick to reassure residents they could “sleep safely in their beds” because the river and rainfall are closely monitored, while urging better evacuation plans and information signs for tourists.The community is not living with fear, says Janelle Shaw, a Franz Josef resident and chair of the Glacier Country Tourism Group. But it is becoming increasingly frustrated at the lack of action. “We’re three years on from when a similar report was released, and we have made no further progress.”
Related: Many of New Zealand’s glaciers could disappear in a decade, scientists warn
For years, Shaw, alongside the residents and community association, has lobbied authorities to include the community in its planning.

“It has to be something that’s happening with the community rather than something that’s happening to the community,” she said, adding the Westland District Council’s new working group, which is supposed to include residents, is a good first step.

Braided rivers move large amounts of gravel and sediment downstream, but in narrowed rivers, the gravel builds upwards, instead of spreading out. The Waiho riverbed is rising about 20 centimetres a year. A large amount of sediment accumulating near the glacier could accelerate the problem if a storm pushes it downstream.

Since the 1980s, stopbanks – a long mound of gravel and soil that limits water spreading on to land – have been erected to contain the river, to make way for land-use such as building, farming and infrastructure. The rising riverbed makes stopbanks more vulnerable to flooding.
“Now the bed of the river is perched two metres above the land adjacent to the river, in the vicinity of the township,” Fuller says.

In 2023, the advisory group found the river was carving out a new channel, north of Franz Josef village. It recommended a 10-year plan to give the river room to move and lessen flood risk. But in September, the group found the river is changing much faster than initially predicted, despite a period of relatively quiet weather.

Franz Josef has long discussed the possibility of relocating the village, but the advisory group recommends first releasing the river’s southern stopbanks to allow the water to fan out and slow the rate of riverbed rise.
It would buy the village time, but requires relocating the highway, wastewater infrastructure and landfills, and submerging swathes of private farmland at a cost of more than $200m (£83m).
Westland District’s mayor, Helen Lash, says the prospect of releasing the river is “very raw” for the community.

“These homes and farms are where they live, what they have invested in and brought their families up in,” Lash says. “It’s a damn hard conversation to have with anyone but it is something we have to look at … if we are to protect the northern side of the town.”
Lash has formed a working group in response to the report, with relevant agencies, local authorities and the community aiming to present a plan to the government in early 2027.

A future government – which will be confirmed when the country’s election results are finalised on 27 November – will decide how to manage the situation. Simon Watts, the minister for local government and climate change, has said authorities are working on legislation to ensure councils are creating adaptation plans for areas exposed to natural hazards.
But Fuller is concerned the government is not acting with enough urgency and pointed to January’s deadly landslide in Tauranga – a known hazard before disaster struck – as a warning.
“We cannot allow that to happen at Franz Josef,” he says. “We know about the risk. We’ve got a solution. It requires investment. There’s no need for anyone to lose life here.”

articles.title: Butt of the joke: Trump impersonator mocks president at Canada press dinner
articles.summary: Carney watches on as comedian lampoons US leader and his interest in men’s backsides at correspondents’ event Ottawa
body: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.

With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex Canada.
“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”
The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.

He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”
Related: Trump forced to play good sport at correspondents’ dinner – but it couldn’t last

He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.
The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.
Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.
At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”
Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.
The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.

“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”

He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.

The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

articles.title: Israel seeks to jail Palestinian student activist without trial after dorm arrest
articles.summary: Mahdi Tounsi appeared with visible bruising after being interrogated by police on his association with Israeli-Palestinian organisations
body: Israeli professors, students and rights activists are calling for the immediate release of Mahdi Tounsi, a sociology student at Jerusalem’s Hebrew University who has been held without charge for more than two weeks after he was seized from his dorm room.

The detention comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.
Police took Tounsi, 26, a criminology and sociology student from East Jerusalem who is active in Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, from his dorm room on 8 November.
When he appeared by video link at a court hearing on 19 November he had visible bruises on his face, did not have the glasses he needs to see properly, and his hair and beard had been shaved.

Tounsi told his lawyer that police beat him in the dorm, in the patrol car and at the police station, Israeli media reported. Interrogators questioned him about his activism with Israeli-Palestinian organisations Standing Together and Ir Amim.
Both groups called for his immediate release and warned against using security agencies to silence political activity and critical speech.

“[This] could happen to any student and any one of us, especially in a month when the government is persecuting Arab citizens, from [journalist] Abed Abu Shehadeh to the leaders of Arab political parties,” Standing Together said in a statement, calling on the university to intervene to ensure a fair judicial process.

Ir Amim described Tounsi as thoughtful, gentle and a valued partner “in movements bringing Palestinians and Israelis together”, in a statement that also warned of “serious concerns for his safety, wellbeing, and right to due process”.

After losing the election, Netanyahu and his allies weaponised false accusations of mass fraud – Israel’s election commission validated the results – in an attempt to hold on to power by delegitimising the votes of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
The prime minister has also been accused of politicising security institutions in his campaign against Palestinian-led parties, and fostering a rise in racist rhetoric.

When police powers to hold Tounsi under the original arrest warrant expired last week, they submitted an order to hold him without trial in administrative detention, signed by the defence minister, Israel Katz.

The administrative detention law allows Israel to hold individuals for up to six months without charging them or allowing them to see evidence against them, although it has to be presented in a closed court.
Because the Shin Bet security force did not send a representative to the hearing on Tounsi’s detention last week, it was postponed until Tuesday.

Ahead of the court hearing, Jewish and Palestinian students demonstrated at universities across the country, including Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, with signs including “Free Mahdi” and “Kidnapping Palestinians will not silence justice”.
The university authorities did not inform his family, and his detention only came to light after concerned friends reported him missing.

Hebrew University said in a statement that it was notified about the arrest shortly before police seized Tounsi, that no university representatives were present when he was detained and police afterwards said the arrest took place “without unusual incidents”.
It did not directly address the allegations of police violence, his visible bruising, the shaving of his head and beard, removal of his glasses or the shifting legal framework.

“The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings,” the statement said.
“We are concerned for his wellbeing,” the statement added, saying the university hoped “that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process”.
Israeli police did not respond to requests for comment about Tounsi’s detention.

Tounsi is a resident of East Jerusalem, not a Palestinian citizen of Israel. Palestinians holding that status can move freely inside Israel and Jerusalem but are stateless and can not vote in Israeli national elections.

articles.title: If Trump, Xi and Putin are carving up the pudding, who gets the sixpence?
articles.summary: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Rafael Behr on the Shenzhen summit, where the three world leaders met without a place at the table for Europe
body: Rafael Behr (Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe, 18 November) draws parallels between the Shenzhen summit and Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin and Franklin D Roosevelt meeting at Yalta. I see it as bringing us a step closer to George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, in which the world is divided into three superstates: Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia.

We already have the surveillance in the form of CCTV, facial-recognition technology and email trawling. Daily we witness the rewriting of history. We could be sleepwalking into a situation from which we will be unable to escape.Andy FazakerleyIrby, Wirral

• Rafael Behr says: “The image of three leaders calibrating the balance of global power has been compared to Yalta, February 1945”. In the absence of Ukrainians, a more accurate comparison would be Munich, September 1938, where the fate of Czechoslovakia was decided without Czech participation.Peter DavisWelwyn, Hertfordshire

• I cannot be the only one who, on seeing the pictures of Xi, Putin and Trump meeting in Shenzhen, thought of James Gillray’s 1805 cartoon The Plumb-pudding in Danger, depicting William Pitt the Younger and Napoleon Bonaparte carving up the globe between them. I wonder who will end up with the silver sixpence?Catherine RoseOlney, Buckinghamshire

• Trump, Xi and Putin’s summit’s group photo makes me despair. This has been an attempt to give credibility to Putin and Trump’s warmongering. How dare they have the audacity to make a “joint peace declaration”. As my mother used to say when seeing shady people, “Would you trust them to take you across the road”?Chris WaltersBuxton, Derbyshire
