articles.title: Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear
articles.summary: Letters: There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg
body: Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector (‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation.Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign, initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development.Controversy over datacentres in Sweden’s north reflect wider debate about resource extraction for the green and technological transitions, and the worry that Sweden is becoming an “electricity colony” of big tech, providing cheap, green energy while the economic benefits are realised elsewhere.At the same time, Sweden-based researchers, such as Julia Velkova, and Jutta Haider and Malte Rödl, have argued that the sustainability of digital infrastructure cannot be reduced to carbon emissions and technological efficiency. Datacentres place high demands on electricity grids, necessitating government investment and compromising access for other industries, communities and public services. While these direct impacts of datacentres are important, so too are the downstream consequences that they overshadow, including how digital services promote climate disinformation and unsustainable mass consumption.Sweden’s renewable energy infrastructure does not make datacentre development environmentally or politically unproblematic, but contributes to distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources.Rather than presenting Sweden as an exception to the growing politicisation of datacentres, we should recognise how these conflicts emerge differently in different places, shaped by their histories, infrastructures and political economies.James White and Nora SöderbergDepartment of Technology and Society, Lund University

articles.title: Leaked data shows more than 1,000 Russian military suicides during Ukraine war
articles.summary: Exclusive: Figures from cache of 11m death certificates reveal suicides account for about a regiment of Russia’s war dead
body: In late October 2024, Alexei Bolgov, a sergeant guarding a military headquarters in the occupied Donetsk region, told his wife, Natalya, over the phone: “It’s horrific, what’s going on here. I’ll tell you when I get back.”

He never made it home. Five weeks later, shortly after turning 29, Bolgov walked about 300 metres from his unit’s command post near the village of Stepove into woodland and shot himself, according to a written account by his commander seen by the Guardian.
“On the day of his death, Bolgov was in a withdrawn state,” his commander wrote.

Bolgov is one of more than 1,000 Russian soldiers recorded as having died by suicide since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to confidential data from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, analysed by the Guardian.

The deaths of a further 885 soldiers in or near Ukraine were recorded as firearm-related injuries of “undetermined intent”, a classification that experts say can conceal suicides and that was used in several cases independently identified by the Guardian as suicides.
Taken together, the suicides amount to approximately a Russian regiment of dead.

The data, which analysts say almost certainly underestimates the true number of suicides, offers a rare, previously unreported glimpse of the strain on Russia’s armed forces nearly five years into a war in which heavy losses and harsh discipline have sapped morale.
Suicides among soldiers are a feature of most wars. A New York Times investigation found that at least 158 active-duty US army soldiers died by suicide in 2023.

But in Russia’s army, military analysts say, the problem is compounded by intense pressure from fellow soldiers and commanders, as well as fear of being sent on extremely dangerous combat missions. Contracts that in effect leave soldiers with no way out of the war add to the sense of desperation.

“There’s clearly a lot of coercion used by the Russian military to force people to go forward. In some cases, they will abuse them, torture them, use different types of physical abuse,” said Rob Lee, a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute. “So it’s not surprising that some guys commit suicide,” he added.
The figures come from a cache of more than 11m death certificates obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacking group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow.
The Kremlin does not publish data on suicides in the military and treats casualty figures as a state secret.

Of the 1,087 suicides by military personnel identified by the Guardian, at least 614 took place in occupied areas of Ukraine or Russian regions bordering it, mainly Belgorod and Bryansk. A further 113 records did not specify a location of death.
More than half of suicides involved firearms – particularly those near the frontlines. The deaths occurred at military camps, combat positions, training grounds and private homes.
Of those suicides that took place in the war zone, 43 were young soldiers aged 18 or 19.

The figures also include 108 men under 25 who died by suicide elsewhere in Russia away from the front. Some are likely to have been conscripts, who are not formally sent to fight in Ukraine but have often been pressed to sign contracts that allow them to be deployed.

Recorded military suicides have risen as the war has gone on, from more than 50 in 2022 to more than 200 in 2024, peaking at 365 in 2025 – mirroring Russia’s overall death toll. In 2026 – despite records being incomplete and lagging behind the battlefield reality – the database already records almost 300 suicides, the second highest total for any year of the war so far.
Activists and lawyers who work with Russian deserters believe the real number is higher.
“I would say it is a low estimate,” said Ivan Chuvilyaev, a spokesperson for Idite Lesom, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert. “Obviously, it is a lot more.”
He described the frontline as “a tin can” from which little information escapes. “Any Rosstat statistic, like any statistic relating to the war, is just reports passed up the chain.
“A man can kill himself, and on paper he is a hero. His parents might even be sent some medal,” Chuvilyaev said.
Officials, he added, had little interest in an accurate count, as the figures would be scrutinised further up the chain of command.

Chuvilyaev and Lee also suggested that most cases in which Russian soldiers took their own lives on the battlefield, often after being wounded or as a Ukrainian drone approached, would probably be recorded as combat deaths rather than suicides. Such incidents have been documented in numerous grim videos from the front.
The gaps are visible in the Rosstat data.

Sergei Savenok, a 62-year-old lieutenant colonel from the Irkutsk region, volunteered in September 2022. Before leaving for the front, he is seen in a video clip taking to the stage of his local community centre to address the men heading off with him. “I’m from Donbas myself. Let’s fucking smash them, lads! That’s all!” he shouted, to applause.

He was found shot dead in occupied Luhansk region in July 2023. His wife, Yelena was informed by officials that his death was suicide, but he does not appear among the suicides in the Rosstat records.
A certificate matching his date of birth instead records a death from injury resulting from the discharge of a handheld firearm, with undetermined intent.
The Guardian was able to identify 1,038 military related deaths with similar causes – 885 of which took place in Ukraine or a bordering region of Russia.
Nor does Alexander Lazor, a 21-year-old private who died near the village of Solodke in Donetsk region in the summer of 2022, appear among the suicides in the records.
His family was told he was killed in combat, and in Rosstat data he is listed to have succumbed to “injuries due to warfare caused by firearms”.
But two soldiers who served alongside Lazor told the Guardian that members of their unit had been informed he had taken his own life.

“Our whole unit was told he killed himself. Perhaps, they decided to cover it up so that our unit doesn’t look bad,” said one of the soldiers, who spoke on condition of anonymity, speculating about why his comrade’s death had not been officially recorded as a suicide.
The suicides are just one sign of an army under strain.

By the end of May 2025, Russian military courts had received cases against 20,662 men for refusing to serve, most for going absent without leave, according to the independent outlet Mediazona. IStories verified this data and found at least 49,000 servicemen of the Russian armed forces had been declared deserters or Awol.
Thoughts of suicide were common among the soldiers Idite Lesom helped to desert, Chuvilyaev said.
“Of course they appear,” he said. “It’s the next stop, after a man realises where he has ended up.”

• In the UK, Combat Stress is a charity offering mental health support for military veterans. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

articles.title: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
articles.summary: Exclusive: Analysis gives most detailed picture yet of the nearly 500,000 Russian losses in Ukraine since 2022
body: Alexander Korepanov signed up to fight in August 2023. He was wounded twice and twice sent back to the front. On 11 May 2025, after 20 months at war, he was killed in the village of Uspenovka, near the eastern Ukrainian city of Pokrovsk, aged 52.
More than 5,000 died with him that week.

The Russian army was losing a staggering 720 men every 24 hours, the highest rate of the war, and at least a third of them were killed around Pokrovsk, where Moscow had thrown tens of thousands of troops into its spring offensive.

The figure comes from a cache of more than 11m death certificates obtained by the hacking group Cyber Partisans, which is linked to the Belarusian opposition, and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow.
Analysed in depth by the Guardian, they give the most detailed picture yet of Russia’s losses in Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Among them, the Guardian identified more than 460,000 deaths linked to the war between the start of the invasion in February 2022 and September 2026. War became the leading cause of death in Russian men under 65 last year.

“There was always sort of an unknown X factor: how many Russian deaths are we missing? And that turned out to be much much more,” said Janis Kluge, a Russia expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, who has closely tracked military deaths.
Militaries typically expect about three wounded for every soldier killed. But Kluge said the data suggested Russia could have more soldiers killed in action than severely wounded.
“This tells you something about this war and the way that it’s fought,” Kluge said.

For all those losses, the frontline has barely moved. Since the start of 2023, Russia has gained about 8,000 sq km, less than 1.5% of Ukraine’s territory, according to data from the Ukrainian monitoring group DeepState.
Stuck on the frontline, Russia has this year turned to destroying Ukraine’s economy and making life in its cities unlivable, in an attempt to force Kyiv into accepting its terms for peace.
Russia’s defence ministry has not updated its official death toll since September 2022, when it said 5,937 servicemen had been killed, and Moscow treats its casualty numbers as a military secret.

The records analysed by the Guardian, compiled by Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, from civil registry offices across the country, show a war that grew steadily more lethal, peaking dramatically in 2025, with little territorial gain for Moscow.

Almost 20,000 deaths were recorded during the first year of the invasion and 50,000 in 2023. In 2024 the toll more than doubled, to more than 134,000 and it rose a further 52% a year later, to close to 200,000, the deadliest year of the war: about 548 men a day, against an average of about 277 since the invasion began.

The scale dwarfs anything suffered by Russia or the Soviet Union since the second world war. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers were killed over the nine years of the Soviet war in Afghanistan, according to official figures; in the worst year, 1984, the toll was about 2,300.
In Ukraine in 2025, Russia was losing that many men roughly every four days.

The comparison with recent western wars is starker still. In the single week that began on 5 May 2025, the Russian army lost more men than the US did in eight years in Iraq, where roughly 4,500 American troops died. About 2,400 US service members perished in two decades in Afghanistan.

The real toll is likely to be higher. The deaths of missing soldiers are often registered months or years later, when bodies are recovered or courts declare men dead, and the records thin out sharply in 2026, even though the fighting has remained exceptionally deadly. Nor does the database capture every death, with some never registered or soldiers missing.

The analysis includes death certificates classified as war-related or where conflict is mentioned as a cause of death – a count which may include some civilians. It also includes all deaths where the employment was marked as military – but excludes any certificates from non-combat age people.
The losses are deepening a demographic crisis the Kremlin has struggled for years to reverse, with consequences likely to be felt for generations.

In 2025, war became the leading cause of death for men under the age of 65. Of the death certificates with recorded cause, 29% mentioned war, followed by 26% of deaths due to circulatory diseases and 12% from external causes, such as accidents, assaults or medical complications. More than half a million Russians have also left the country since the invasion.

“We’ve been predicting demographic doom for Russia for a few decades, and somehow the catastrophe never materialised,” said Judyth Twigg, a professor of global health at Virginia Commonwealth University in the US.

“But the current situation really does look qualitatively different … Today’s losses are a direct consequence of regime policy: combat deaths, political emigration, foregone births, healthcare budgets raided to fund [military] signing bonuses and death payouts.”
The certificates record where most soldiers died, down to the village, from mid-2023 onwards.
The records show how much Russia has paid for every kilometre gained on a handful of narrow fronts, above all in the slow advance through the fortified mining towns north-west of Donetsk.

Almost 116,000 of the deaths – over a quarter of the total with a known recorded location – occurred in Pokrovsk district, which takes in both Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, scenes of two of the longest and bloodiest battles of the war.
Pokrovsk itself, a coalmining town of 60,000 people before the war, covers less than 30 sq km. More Russian soldiers have died in the district around it than Ukrainians lived in the city itself.
After neighbouring Avdiivka fell in February 2024, Russian troops took 21 months to cover 39km (24 miles) to the edge of Pokrovsk, according to the Institute for the Study of War.
In that time, about 88,700 Russian soldiers were recorded as dying in the district, more than 2,200 for every kilometre gained.
By September 2024, Russia’s gains formed a bulge of fields, slag heaps and mining villages about 30km long and 20km wide.

The rest of the front is traceable through the data too. Recorded deaths in Russia’s Kursk region rose from 12 in July 2024 to close to 1,200 in August, when Ukraine launched its cross-border incursion into the area, and reached more than 2,400 in December as Moscow fought to retake the territory.

The losses are eroding Russia’s ability to mount new offensives, and help explain why its army looks set to fail to carry out Putin’s order to capture the whole of the Donbas region by the end of the year.

“If we compare the death data with Russia’s official recruitment rates, it becomes clear that Russia’s military has a manpower problem,” said Kluge. “The absolutely horrible losses combined with slower recruitment rates apparently forced Russia to slow down its attacks in 2026 already,” he added.

In 2018, Putin spoke of Russians looking forward to a “well-deserved retirement”, when they could devote more time to their families, children and grandchildren. Eight years later, more and more older Russian men are dying on the battlefields of Ukraine.
The average age at death has risen from 34 in 2022 to close to 40 this year.
Almost a fifth of the soldiers killed in 2026 whose age is recorded were over 50, against 6% in the first year of the war. Across the war, men aged 35 to 44 make up a third of the dead.

The shift reflects how Russia has filled its military ranks. Rather than order a second mobilisation – the first, seven months after the start of the full-scale invasion, in September 2022, was deeply unpopular – the Kremlin has relied on cash bonuses to attract volunteers, and the money has often appealed most to older men such as Korepanov.
From the start of the war, the Kremlin has sought to keep the cost out of sight in Moscow and St Petersburg, where discontent poses the greatest political risk.

The losses fall hardest on Russia’s poor, far-flung regions, many of them home to large ethnic minority populations. The eight Russian regions with the most poverty recorded a military death rate four times higher than those with the least, recording more than 10 deaths per 1,000 men aged 18-69, compared with fewer than three per 1,000.

In at least 19 Russian regions, most of them in the far east, more than half of deaths of men under 50 in 2025 were due to the war. The figures are based on place of birth, using records where a cause of death was given.

In the Jewish autonomous oblast, a region in eastern Russia bordering China where about a fifth of the population lived in poverty in 2022, which despite its Soviet-era name is less than 1% Jewish, war was listed as the cause of more than three-quarters of recorded deaths of men under 50 last year.

The highest death rate was recorded in Zabaykalsky Krai, another region bordering China thousands of miles from the front, where about one in six people live below the poverty line. Since the beginning of the war, 32 men aged 18 to 69 born in the region have died per 1,000 population, compared with one per 1,000 in St Petersburg and Moscow, where less than 5% live in poverty.

As losses have mounted, Moscow has cast its net even wider. Alongside the cash bonuses offered at home, Russia has recruited heavily among central Asian migrant workers inside the country and, through networks of murky middlemen abroad, from as far afield as Nepal, India, Cuba and Kenya.
Many recruits were lured by promises of high pay, Russian citizenship or civilian jobs, only to find themselves at the front.
The Guardian identified more than 7,300 probable foreign soldiers among the dead, not counting Ukrainians. That includes 2,700 who were born abroad but have no recorded citizenship.

Many come from the large central Asian migrant workforce Russia has courted with fast-track citizenship in exchange for service, with more than three-quarters coming from former Soviet republics, mainly from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Belarus.

But the analysis identified foreign fighters from 78 other countries beyond the former USSR, including 440 whose citizenship was from an African country – such as Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt, and about 200 from South America, most of them from Colombia and Cuba.

The records miss what is likely to be the deadliest foreign contingent of all. North Korea sent more than 10,000 troops to help Russia drive Ukrainian forces out of the Kursk region in late 2024 and 2025. South Korea’s national intelligence service estimates about 2,000 of them have been killed, and about 6,000 killed or wounded in total.

The foreign soldiers arrived late. Of those whose date of death is recorded, three-quarters were killed in 2025 or later. Every Colombian death with a recorded date falls within that period, as recruiters turned to Latin America to make up for losses at home.
What the scale of the losses will mean for Russians’ attitudes to the war in the long run remains unclear.
In interviews, many relatives of the dead said their grief had only hardened their support for the war. Several insisted that Russia must fight on, so that the sacrifice would not have been in vain.
State propaganda has cast the fallen as heroes, holding up their deaths as a reason for Russians to stand united behind Putin and the army.

The few who once spoke out against the war have mostly been jailed or forced to leave the country. The last group publicly protesting against the war, Put Domoi (Way Home), a movement of wives and mothers of mobilised men, was criminalised in 2024.
One woman who was once among its most outspoken members said she now feared for her life.
“I don’t have emotions any more; I am numb at this point. Just a question,” she asked rhetorically. “Is it worth it?”

articles.title: Germany taking seriously reports Russia may be planning to launch nuclear weapons into space
articles.summary: Move would breach nuclear weapons treaties and reports come amid rising concerns over militarisation of space
body: The German government has said it is taking very seriously reports that Russia may be planning to launch a satellite armed with a ⁠nuclear weapon ⁠into ​space later this year.

The move – if confirmed – would be a breach of 1967 Outer Space treaty of which Moscow is a signatory as well the 1963 Partial Nuclear Test Ban treaty – which prohibit the placing of nuclear weapons in Earth’s orbit and test detonations in space.

The reports by a group of German media outlets, based on what they said were assessments by western intelligence agencies, come amid a recent rise in concern over the increasing militarisation of space which had the US Air Force secretary, Troy Meink, admit for the first time in September that Washington had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons”.

Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces have exchanged ⁠intelligence showing that a Russian satellite, named Sputnik-S, ​was assembled several ‌years ago ‌and is stationed in the Moscow region, ‌a report by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung said.
According to the reports, warnings in early November said the satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.

“No, we haven’t seen ‌the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ ​and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that ⁠it’s certainly hardly worth ​taking ​them seriously,” Kremlin spokesperson ​Dmitry Peskov told ​reporters.

The Russian embassy in Berlin said it was not aware of any such plans describing the reports as “unfounded allegations regarding the space activities of the Russian Federation” and calling them “part of a propaganda campaign”.
Moscow’s space measures, the embassy added, proceed “in accordance with international obligations” and serve “exclusively peaceful purposes”.
Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, said on Monday that the alliance was ⁠constantly assessing its deterrence and defence situation.

“I can assure ⁠you, we will always make ​sure that ‌we defend every inch ‌of Nato territory. And that ‌includes making sure that we are safe when it comes to the space element,” he told a joint press ‌conference with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz.

In 2024, Russia denied assertions by ​US officials that Moscow was developing a weapon that could destroy enemy satellites by setting off a nuclear explosion in ⁠space and triggering an electromagnetic pulse (EMP) to disable the electronic systems of nearby satellites.

US officials have alleged that Russia ​has ​for years been developing ​a nuclear weapon capable of ​destroying ‌entire satellite networks, ​such ​as SpaceX’s vast Starlink internet system that Ukrainian troops have been using.
Concern has been mounting in recent years in Europe and the US that Russia has been seeking to develop an anti-satellite weapon system which experts believe would probably employ an EMP wave.

Two years ago, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, denied the claim after then US president Joe Biden’s national security spokesperson John Kirby confirmed that the Russian Federation had been developing a “troubling” anti-satellite weapon.
“We’re not talking about a weapon that can be used to attack human beings or cause physical destruction here on Earth,” Kirby said.
Biden told reporters in 2024 that he believed Russia was developing the “capacity to launch a system into space that could theoretically do something that was damaging … my hope is it will not”.

While EMPs can occur naturally, it has long been understood that nuclear detonation has the ability to harm electronic systems, including energy networks, with both the US and Russia conducting high altitude tests in the early 1960s.

There has been increasing discussion over fears that Russia may be planning to place a nuclear weapon in space. Germany’s top military space commander earlier this year said he could not rule out that Russia was working on technology to place a nuclear warhead in space, warning that such a move could cripple satellite services and make parts of the orbit unusable for decades.

“At the very top end of escalation, there is the suspicion that Russia may be working on technology to place a nuclear explosive device in orbit,” Maj Gen Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, said in an interview with Politico.

Asked whether he considered that realistic, Traut said: “I cannot rule it out.” He added that a nuclear detonation in space could impact up to a third of satellites in low Earth orbit with massive global consequences.

Suspicions over Russia’s ambitions to place weapons in space were given fresh scrutiny in 2022 with the launch of the Kosmos 2553 test satellite, which US and intelligence sources suggested could be a dummy run for the deployment of a nuclear weapon in space.

articles.title: Twenty Gaza students due to leave for Ireland after winning visa battle
articles.summary: Group’s evacuation follows campaign to overturn decision to deny visas to more than 60 students from territory
body: Twenty students from Gaza are to travel to Ireland to take up scholarships after winning a battle for visas that undercut the Irish government’s reputation as a champion of Palestinians.

The group is due to leave the territory on Monday under strict Israeli controls and travel via Jordan to Dublin to take up places at Irish universities. Another group is expected to follow next month.
The evacuation comes after a four-month campaign to overturn a decision by the Irish Department of Justice to deny visas to more than 60 students in Gaza who had been offered scholarships in Ireland.
The decision dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused the department of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians.

The government backed down last week after a Dublin high court ordered the department to reconsider the decision. The minister for justice, Jim O’Callaghan, approved 48 visas. The first group is expected to arrive on Tuesday, with the remainder coming in late December.

“It’s a mix of feelings I still can’t fully describe,” Amir Alareer, 26, who is to study cybersecurity and artificial intelligence at University College Dublin, said via email on the eve of his departure from Gaza.

“There is hope and relief after months of waiting and fighting for this moment. But it is hard to feel complete joy when I am leaving my family behind in Gaza, and when 28 of my fellow students, who hold the same visas and share the same dreams, are still here waiting.”

The students originally expected to come in summer, and had supporting paperwork from Irish universities, but in July the Department of Justice rejected the visa applications. “The refusals hit us hard,” said Alareer.

The department demanded bank statements, proof of intention to return and other documents and said any appeal would have to be made by post, saying screening and verification were integral to the immigration system.

The students said such documents had not previously been requested and that Gaza’s banking and postal service had been destroyed. Ivana Bacik, a legislator and leader of the Labour party, accused the department of using “spurious reasons” amid a hardening of immigration policy.

Alareer helped to lead a campaign from Gaza that was backed in Ireland by demonstrators, a petition and an open letter signed by actors, writers and artists including Hozier, Nicola Coughlan and the rap group Kneecap. “Running a campaign from Gaza, through blackouts and displacement, was not easy, but I knew that if we stayed silent, our case would be forgotten,” said Alareer.

In October, the high court ruled that there were “significant and demonstrable errors” in the refusal of a visa to Shaymaa Abudalu, a 20-year-old who had been offered an engineering scholarship at University College Cork, and who was the lead case in a batch of similar lawsuits. A high court judge welcomed the decision last week to grant 48 visas and said “huge progress” had been made.
Among the students are five members of a dance troupe who have been offered places at the Irish World Academy of Music and Dance at the University of Limerick.

Alareer, who studied engineering at Al-Azhar University – Gaza, said Israel’s attacks on Gaza had destroyed his home and displaced the family several times. “The hardest experience of all was the famine, when we couldn’t find even a single kilo of flour.” Floods have impeded recent relief efforts.

His family was proud of his scholarship, he said, but saying goodbye would be hard. “They are happy that I finally have this opportunity, but leaving them behind after everything we have been through together is incredibly difficult.”

After studying software and innovation in Dublin, Alareer plans to return to Al-Azhar University and establish a cybersecurity department. “I want to build a generation of Palestinian engineers and researchers who can protect our digital future. Gaza will be rebuilt, and its systems must be rebuilt securely, by its own people.”

articles.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.summary: Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship
body: Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Institute for the Study of War said the Merkury had stopped over for several days, under a cooperation agreement, to refuel and resupply as it escorted Russian cargo ships that could carry military supplies en route to Russia.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts to use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.

The confirmation that Ukraine was behind the attacks was condemned by the UN-recognised government in Tripoli. It said Libya rejected ⁠any foreign ⁠military ​operations on its territory or in its waters.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said Ukraine’s strikes in the Mediterranean “were exceptionally brazen and provocative”.

He added: “The question now is how Russia will retaliate,. Perhaps even more pressing is how the [Hafter] family will respond, given how traumatic the scale of the destruction has been for eastern Libyan authorities.”
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

articles.title: From mocked to mainstream: how Spain’s far-right Vox transformed its fortunes
articles.summary: Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government
body: Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain. The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil.

Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament.

Until that moment, the prevailing wisdom had been that Spain’s experiences of the Franco dictatorship had inoculated the country against the far right, and that Vox was a tiny, fringe outfit whose prospects were terminally limited after it had picked up just 0.2% of the vote in the 2016 general election.

Fast-forward to late 2026 and the horseman seems less comical still. Vox, now the third largest party in Spain, is poised to pick up almost 20% of the vote in the snap general election on 29 November and, very possibly, to form a coalition government with the conservative People’s party (PP).

Abascal is going all out as the campaign enters its final days, peppering his patriotic appeals with familiar, baseless conspiracy theories. Last week he suggested that the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, was conspiring with dark forces to undermine democracy and change the country’s demographic makeup.
“The next elections may be the last that Spaniards get to decide,” he posted on X. “That’s what Sánchez and his accomplices at home and abroad are working toward … Vote so you don’t get replaced.”

How did Vox’s fortunes transform so massively and so quickly? The party was founded in late 2013 by disenchanted PP members who felt the conservatives had grown too indulgent of the demands of Basque and Catalan nationalist parties, but it struggled to make its mark. The highlight of its early years, during which it relied on hefty sum donated by the Iranian exile group the National Council of Resistance of Iran, was unfurling a large Spanish flag on the Rock of Gibraltar.

All that changed in the autumn of 2017 when a Catalan push for independence pitched Spain into crisis and left the PP government looking soft and ill-prepared. The crisis proved a godsend for Vox, simultaneously vindicating its distrust of Catalan and Basque nationalist parties and allowing it to position itself as an uncompromising defender of Spanish unity.

“Vox’s initial growth was driven by a reaction to Catalan nationalism – specifically, the sense around 2017 that Spain might fall apart,” says Miguel González, an El País journalist who covers Vox and the author of a new book, The Extremist Galaxy: Funders, Allies and Strategies of the New Far Right.
It gave Vox the profile it needed to pursue what González considers its most significant move: dragging immigration into mainstream politics and forcing a rattled PP to lurch further to the right.

“It was only an issue in a few specific places with high levels of immigration – such as El Ejido in Almería, or certain areas in Murcia,” González says. “[But] Vox has managed to put this issue on the political agenda, and, what’s more, the PP has gradually come to adopt some of their positions.”

This summer’s mass influx into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, when more than 80,000 men, women and children crossed over from Morocco, is a case in point. Abascal called it “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco”, while the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo urged the expulsion of all who had entered, regardless of their age and individual circumstances.

The PP’s efforts to stop its voters slipping into the embrace of its far-right rival have led it into all sorts of contortions. Although Feijóo’s predecessor, Pablo Casado, famously rounded on Vox in 2020, accusing Abascal and co of peddling a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, the PP has repeatedly entered into regional coalition governments with Vox and now runs four of Spain’s autonomous regions with the party.
Related: Will Spain’s snap election in November bring a far-right party into government?

Vicente Valentim, a professor of political science at Spain’s IE University and the author of The Normalisation of the Radical Right, says that when centre-right parties adopt the language and postures of the far right, they end up legitimising it.

“After the initial normalisation moment when these parties first become successful – entering parliament etc – there’s a second step,” he says. “The centre right moves closer to them, starts speaking the same way that they do, starts going into coalitions.”

This can prove electorally expensive, he says. “The PP has moved closer to Vox, and when you have two parties that have such similar views on an issue as important as immigration, [some] voters simply prefer the original to the copy, and so they’re going to vote for Vox.”

Alongside a fixation on immigration, Vox has also brought its predilection for hate figures into the mainstream of Spanish politics – be they the secessionist former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont, the former leader of the leftwing Podemos Pablo Iglesias, or Sánchez.
“Vox talks about traitors and about criminals,” says González. “What Vox is doing isn’t offering political assessments, it’s making legal judgments.”

Abascal’s loathing of Sánchez is well documented – in 2023, the Vox leader said a day would come when the Spanish people would “want to see [Sánchez] strung up by his feet” – and his party’s manifesto vows to “undertake legal proceedings to have Sánchez and his government prosecuted for treason and crimes against the security of the state, based on their actions during the invasion of Ceuta”.
The party’s increasingly strident language has been matched by a more recent refusal to sever ties with some of the more extreme figures in its ranks and in its orbit.

In the run-up to the first of the two general elections in 2019, Vox was forced to drop the historian and commentator Fernando Paz from its list of candidates after Jewish groups complained about his “denialist and revisionist” approach to the Holocaust. Today he sits on the honorary board of the Foundation for the Defence of the Spanish Nation, a Vox-aligned platform of which Abascal is a co-founder and board member.

One pro-Israel lobbying group has expressed concerns in the past about Jordi de la Fuente, a Vox member and former neo-Nazi party leader who heads the Solidarity trade union, which was created by Vox. De la Fuente, who is awaiting trial for his alleged role in a violent attack on a centre housing unaccompanied migrant children in 2019, is standing as Vox’s candidate in Tarragona. Vox has insisted its candidate is innocent of a charge of “inciting hatred, hostility, violence or discrimination on the grounds of national origin”.

Alejandro Baer, a sociologist at the Spanish National Research Council who specialises in memory, genocide studies and contemporary Jewish studies, says: “A few years ago, the party was forced to distance itself from them, but now they don’t seem to represent a liability. Vox appears to be sufficiently consolidated and legitimate to openly incorporate people with backgrounds in these extremist spaces.”

Vox’s trajectory is plain to see in Rioja, a small town in the eastern Andalucían province of Almería. Long a socialist stronghold, Rioja was the only municipality where Vox finished first in May’s regional election – a poll that resulted in another PP-Vox coalition, after the conservatives lost their absolute majority. And yet the quiet town, whose palm trees and bougainvillaeas rustle in the warm November breeze, doesn’t exactly have the feel of a far-right frontier. Its divisions appear more generational than political.

Few of the younger people walking down the main road that bisects Rioja are surprised by Vox’s strong showing here. Fewer still appear bothered by Sánchez’s warning that a PP-Vox coalition will “roll back progress” and lead to the loss of hard-won social advances.

“My own ideology tends more to the right,” says Patricio López, 29, who works in an agricultural company. “I’ve noticed that people of my age tend to be more rightwing than leftwing, and I think that’s because they feel like they’ve been shortchanged. Housing, for example, is a much bigger issue for young people than it is for older people. And the left hasn’t looked after young people over the past eight years.”
One older resident, however, believes Vox’s surge in Rioja has more to do with protest votes from the young and the proximity of a large military camp than a rejection of its socialist past.

“I think it was just a gesture of distrust and revenge in the way Spanish politics is these days – it’s pure partisan theatre and it’s all very Game of Thrones,” says Rafael Ruiz Martínez, 63, who works for the local council. But he adds: “For those of us who lived through some of the Franco era, the Vox stuff doesn’t sound good.”
Another younger local man, who prefers not to give his name, agrees many people are sick of traditional politics and of a political class that has failed them.
“I reckon whoever gets in – whatever their political stripe – will do what others have done; they’ll dip into the till,” he says. “But politics is politics and people want a change.”

articles.title: Monday briefing: What could Andy Burnham’s reset mean for the UK?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The UK’s intervention has reopened the debate over a future relationship with the EU, as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions
body: Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday.

That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election.

Putting aside the question of whether a second referendum would merely reopen old wounds, Europe has changed dramatically since 2016, creating new challenges for any government seeking a closer relationship with the EU. For this morning’s newsletter, I discussed these challenges and what they mean for rejoining with Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group and a frequent contributor to the Guardian’s Opinion section. That’s after the headlines.

Cop31 | The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal that “failed to meet the moment” in a dramatic finish to the UN talks in Turkey. The proposed deal failed to endorse a away from fossil fuels that more than 130 countries demanded.
Russia | A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

Weapons| The Red Cross and other rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to properly regulate the development of autonomous weapons. The warning came as the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded without an agreement on an instrument for regulating autonomous weapons.

UK news | Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

West Bank | Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank after dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday.

Three separate deals were announced at Friday’s summit in Brussels: one on food and drink, another on emissions trading, and a third on youth mobility, which will allow British students to work, live, study and travel in the EU and give reciprocal access to EU students in Britain (for a full recap, read Jennifer Rankin and Alexandra Topping’s explainer). Burnham wants to go further, and both he and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, have used the near-identical phrase that all options are “on the table” for Britain’s future relationship with the EU.

You’d be forgiven for feeling weary about revisiting the last decade in British politics. As one Labour MP recently told the Financial Times (£), “nobody is asking for this.” Burnham seems to be testing the ground ahead of a general election, hoping that a campaign to rejoin, or at least move closer to, the EU could plausibly win over progressive defectors.

Still, Friday’s agreement was a reminder of how difficult it is to negotiate with a club of 27. Member states, including France and Italy, issued a statement making it clear that the deal wouldn’t be implemented unless Burnham offered a deal on tuition fees for EU students at British universities. “There’s a fairly strong sense that we’ve reached the end of the incremental style of negotiating,” Mujtaba Rahman tells me. “There isn’t much more for the UK to do before it starts to resemble a cherrypicking state.” And there are other developments that will be on the minds of negotiators and ministers contemplating the UK’s future relationship with Europe.
Has the far right made the idea of European Union membership less attractive?

This is one of the major developments: Europe has become decidedly more right-wing since 2016. Though the European far right lost one of its key figureheads when Viktor Orbán was defeated in the Hungarian elections earlier this year, far-right parties govern in the Czech Republic and Italy, and support for them is rising in Austria and Germany. The proportion of voters in Europe who cast their ballots for far-right parties has grown more than five times since the 1990s, and has increased particularly sharply over the last three years.

Whether this will make rejoining less appealing depends largely on what happens next year in the French elections. Marine Le Pen, who is now favoured to win, wants to slash France’s contribution to the EU budget and drastically downsize the union. It’s possible that a Le Pen presidency could embolden other EU member states to seek closer ties with a pro-European British government, but it’s also possible that Le Pen’s domestic policies, such as reducing the retirement age to 60, could trigger a domestic economic crisis and inflame a conflict between the EU and France, one of its founding member states. “If Marine Le Pen wins, and France tries to enforce a domestic programme that runs in opposition to the EU, then I think a lot of people in the UK will look at the resulting crisis and think, ‘Thank God we’re out of that’,” Mujtaba says.
Is the EU’s new protectionism a reason to rejoin?

The EU’s Made in Europe strategy would have been almost unimaginable a decade ago, when progressives criticised the union for enforcing free-market globalisation on its members and forbidding state aid. The strategy, which uses public money to support goods made by companies in the single market, is a sign of both how isolated the UK has become and how much the world has changed. Burnham is now trying to make “reindustrialisation” part of his agenda at home, but the EU’s initiative is designed to disadvantage countries outside the EU. It risks scuppering his efforts by deindustrialising the UK car industry, which relies on European buyers.

“It’s very hard for the government to influence this because the Made in Europe negotiations are internal to the EU. And it’s very hard for member states to provide any guarantees because there’s no UK guardian at the table,” Mujtaba says. The EU hasn’t included the UK in the scheme, though Friday’s summit promised closer cooperation on steel and electric vehicle supply chains. But that may require the UK to follow EU policies without having any ability to shape them, making the idea of full membership much more appealing.
Would rejoining mean taking a different approach to defence?

This is perhaps the strongest reason of all for rejoining, but it’s also another area where the EU’s approach has evolved significantly over the last decade. “The geopolitical environment is forcing the EU to do a bunch of things the UK has historically taken issue with,” Mujtaba says. “It’s intervening in areas of policy that would have traditionally been the purview of nation states.” In particular, the EU’s Security Action for Europe facility (Safe), a new EU defence fund offering up to €150bn in loans to member states to fund defence investments, shifts defence from a national concern to one of wider European governance.

Britain refused to pay the financial contribution that Brussels wanted for it to participate in the Safe fund, though there are signs that the two sides may still reach a deal. But any campaign to rejoin would need to critically evaluate the deep ties and so-called “special relationship” between the UK and US in light of an EU that has grown to regard the US as an unreliable partner on security.

“The UK isn’t quite as far-reaching in its conclusions about the US,” Mujtaba says. “You don’t hear UK officials talking about the Americans in the same way that European officials are talking about the Americans.”

David Byrne on the great ideas that got away

David Byrne, the frontman of Talking Heads and then as a solo artist, has made some of the greatest albums of all time. He tells Nosheen Iqbal about his new book Sleeping Beauties, in which he explores why so many breakthroughs in science, economics and culture were lost on their initial audience and only later revived and acknowledged to be great.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

David Parr’s days were spent decorating wealthy homes with William Morris’s much-loved textile designs. But by candlelight at night, Parr, a Victorian working-class labourer, would turn to the interiors of his own home, decorating his walls with his own beautiful designs, work that went largely unnoticed during his life.

After his death in 1927, those extraordinary walls in his home on Gwydir Street in Cambridge were thankfully preserved by his granddaughter, Elsie. Today, The David Parr House, as it is now known, is set to be honoured with a blue plaque, which is thought to be the first ever dedicated to a working-class Victorian art-workman.

articles.title: MPs urge Miliband to force UK overseas territories to publish public company registers
articles.summary: Improvements in corporate transparency ‘essential’ amid ‘outright disregard for the will of parliament’, says cross-party group
body: Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency.

Ahead of a meeting between the foreign secretary and overseas territories this week, a cross-party group of MPs from Labour, the Tories, Lib Dems and Greens wrote to Miliband calling on him to mandate public registers of beneficial ownership of companies.

The group, coordinated by the all-party group on anti-corruption (APPG), said an improvement in corporate transparency in the overseas territories was essential after “years of broken promises and missed deadlines from certain jurisdictions, and despite repeated commitments to ending secrecy”.
They said some territories such as Gibraltar, Montserrat and St Helena had successfully opened corporate registers to the public.

But they called out the British Virgin Islands, saying it “in particular continues to let the British family down”. They said the Cayman Islands has raised its search fees to “prohibitive levels”, and Turks and Caicos have introduced huge fines for disclosing information from the register which they said was “undermining the entire purpose of open registers”.
They said that persistent engagement in good faith from the UK government has yielded few results, in the face of “outright disregard for the will of parliament”.

The BVI has a register launched this year which allows people to apply for access to ownership information if they have a “legitimate interest” such as investigating money laundering. A BVI Government spokesperson said: “We are proud of the BVI’s Legitimate Interest Access register introduced earlier this year, which allows for prompt, proportionate access, in line with international standards.

“We continue to work closely with the UK Government, delivering a major governance and regulatory reform programme to support global efforts combatting illicit finance, enforcing sanctions and recovering criminal assets - with significant progress recently recognised by the Financial Action Task Force.”

However, ahead of the meeting, the MPs including former Conservative Foreign Office minister Andrew Mitchell and Labour anti-corruption expert Phil Brickell are asking Miliband to lay an order in council mandating fully public registers of beneficial ownership in jurisdictions that continue to fail to meet their obligations.

They said it was important for UK national security “because continued secrecy undermines our ability to enforce sanctions and leaves us open to hostile state actors and criminal networks”. Second, they said developing countries continue to be destabilised and looted by kleptocrats using Britain’s own offshore financial centres to clean and stash their ill-gotten gains.

Parliament voted for open registers in 2018 and the UK government had expected public access registers to be in place in all overseas territories and crown dependencies by 2023. However, this deadline was not met.

While an order in council to mandate open registers was drafted in 2020, the government said that because there were “firm commitments” from the overseas territories to introduce public registers, the order would not be used. It said it would keep this decision under review.

Brickell, Labour chair of the APPG, said “it should never have come to this but every year of deliberate delay is another year in which kleptocrats, tax dodgers and money launderers can hide behind a British flag”.
“That is a stain on the reputation of our global family. This joint ministerial council must be the moment we finally draw a line under it.”

Mitchell, a Conservative vice-chair of the APPG and former development secretary, said: “When parliament voted for public registers in 2018, it was not making a polite request. It was the clear, cross-party will of the House of Commons, and it should have been respected.

“Instead, money stolen from some of the poorest people on earth is still being hidden behind anonymous companies in British jurisdictions. That money should be building hospitals and schools. It is paying for yachts and mansions instead, and the price is measured in lives. The British family has been patient for long enough. The foreign secretary has the power to act, and I urge him to use it.”

A Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Security is the first duty of any government. Hostile states and malign actors can exploit opaque corporate structures like those in the British Virgin Islands to hide their assets and support activity that threatens our national security.“Ministers are actively considering how best to ensure that, where the risks are greatest, law enforcement agencies have the information they need to progress critical investigations. We will continue ongoing engagement with Overseas Territories on these issues.”

articles.title: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find
articles.summary: Scientific and satellite findings warn of widespread contamination in Gaza, posing grave threats to public health ‘for generations to come’
body: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report.

Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.

Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”

He said the “destruction and contamination of Gaza” have “fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival” and breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins … through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”

In 2025 and earlier this year, the UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. The Israeli mission in Geneva said Israel rejected the commission’s “libellous sham”. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.

Oxfam’s report gives the most comprehensive picture to date of what it calls the “toxic wasteland” created by the Israeli assault which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded at least 175,000, while thousands still remain unaccounted for under the rubble.

Using satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, it concludes contamination in Gaza is “widespread, severe and consequential, with serious implications for public health and civilian survival”.

Behar said: “It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers. In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing.
“Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them.”
He added the “associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks”.

The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that Israel’s military operations have generated more than 61m tonnes of debris across the territory, turning Gaza’s destroyed homes, neighbourhoods and infrastructure into a vast reservoir of potentially hazardous materials.

The report’s author, Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam, said tackling the environmental damage in Gaza will be “highly challenging because contamination is dispersed across the urban rubble, farmland, water systems and soils, while unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas”.

“The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm-reduction measures. Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring and specialised remediation of affected areas from contaminants such as explosive residues, organic pollutants and heavy metals.”
Behar said that as international attention increasingly turned to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought, but as a vital undertaking in parallel.
“Rebuilding Gaza without simultaneously understanding and addressing the extent of environmental contamination risks creating long-term public health consequences for generations to come,” he said.

A spokesperson from the Israeli embassy in the UK questioned the methodology underpinning the report, saying its reliance on satellite imagery and what they described as unverified assumptions “falls short of professional standards”.

They added: “Hamas itself claimed to have excavated more than 500 km of tunnels beneath Gaza, exceeding the total route length of the London Underground. A report on Gaza’s soil and groundwater that fails to examine excavation on that scale is fundamentally incomplete. That omission undermines the credibility of its conclusions.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Race to find survivors after Russian attack on apartment block kills at least 11
articles.summary: Woman and child pulled out alive after overnight strike in Dymer north of Kyiv; UN mission calls for investigation into attack that sank Russian warship in Libya. What we know on day 1,734
body: Rescuers in Ukraine raced on Monday to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike, after overnight attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 14 people. A strike on Dymer, about 45km north of the capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11, according to Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko. He gave the latest toll while saying rescuers ‌had pulled another body ​from the ⁠rubble. The dead included a teenager and a woman in her 40s, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES) said earlier. Tkachenko said rescuers also pulled out people alive from the rubble including a child and a 79-year-old woman. The SES said earlier it was searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”. “When [the explosion came], I literally flipped over in bed,” said Mykola Osadnyi, a relative of some of the missing who lived nearby. “My father-in-law … was screaming: ‘Save me, I’m burning!’” Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets called the attack part of “Russia’s genocidal war against Ukraine”.

In Vyshneve, three people were killed and 15 wounded – including three children – when a Russian strike hit a supermarket, mayor Illya Dikov said. “People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries,” Tkachenko said. One more person was killed when a strike set a private home ablaze in Bila Tserkva, he added. Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukrainian prime minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.

A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck early on Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. The strike – more than 1,000 miles from southern Ukraine – severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government, report Dan Sabbagh and Angelique Chrisafis. Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike. The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the drone attacks and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.

Polish authorities say they have identified three flying objects that hit the country’s south-east as Russian cruise missiles, as Nato prepared to meet about an incident that Polish prime minister Donald Tusk called an “intentional provocation”. The prosecutor’s office in the city of Lublin said on Sunday that examination of fragments of the missiles that fell on Friday in the villages of Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik and Molodycz showed they were all Russian Kh-101 missiles. No one was injured when the missiles hit, though one impact was followed by an explosion and fire. Nato allies will meet in Brussels on Monday to discuss the incident. The missiles fell close to where thousands of troops from the European “coalition of the willing” – set up to support Ukraine – were holding exercises.

Denmark has expelled a Russian official after it said it had thwarted an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian American rapper at a concert on Danish soil. The case took a new twist on Sunday when Polish authorities revealed that the same man, Albert Vasiliev, was allegedly targeted by Moscow’s intelligence services last summer in Poland. Denmark is reportedly expected to ask the European Union this week for more decisive action stemming from the case.

articles.title: Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
articles.summary: No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia
body: A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.
The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.

Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.

Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.

Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.

Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.

Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.
Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.
The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.

The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.
It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.
“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.

HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.
But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.
On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.
The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

articles.title: Let refugees work and contribute to our society
articles.summary: Letters: Shirley Hart urges us to look beyond the labels of ‘asylum seeker’ and ‘refugee’ to see human beings forced to leave their homes. Plus a letter from Steve Wells
body: Congratulations to Zoe Williams on her excellent article (Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human?, 17 November). I am the vice-chair of a charity in Hull that helps asylum seekers and refugees, and I have to say that the “service users” of Welcome House are some of the kindest, most polite and grateful people I have met.

A young man who shared his gloves on a cold winter’s day so that he and his friend could have at least one warm hand. A young woman from Afghanistan who wants to have an education and qualify as a doctor. The group of young men who picked up 20 bags of litter to make Hull, a City of Sanctuary, a cleaner place to live.
Let them work, let them contribute to society – they are some of the most hard-working and resilient people I know.

Look beyond the labels of asylum seeker and refugee, and see the human being who was forced to leave their home to seek safety. What would we do if we found ourselves in the same situation?Shirley Hart Woodmansey, East Yorkshire

• Zoe Williams’s piece, critically, did not use the word “migrant”. This term, especially when often linked with “illegal”, is ultimately dehumanising. It’s now common parlance on mainstream media. Language is important. “Migrant” is insidiously toxic. Refugees seek refuge for all sorts of reasons. Migrants just move, threateningly.Steve WellsClaygate, Surrey
